purpose: This medication is a birth control pill used to prevent pregnancy. It may also be prescribed to help with painful or irregular periods, acne, or symptoms related to endometriosis. Your doctor will let you know the specific reason it was prescribed for you.
how_it_works: This pill contains two hormones — estrogen and progestin — that work together to prevent pregnancy in a few ways. They stop your ovaries from releasing an egg each month, thicken the mucus around your cervix so sperm cannot easily get through, and thin the lining of your uterus. Together, these effects make it very unlikely for pregnancy to occur.
common_side_effects: Some women notice nausea, breast tenderness or swelling, spotting or light bleeding between periods (especially in the first few months), headaches, mood changes, or decreased sex drive. These side effects often improve after the first 2-3 months as your body adjusts.
warnings: Do not take this medication if you smoke and are over 35 years old, as this raises your risk of serious blood clots, stroke, or heart attack. Tell your doctor if you have a history of blood clots, high blood pressure, migraines with aura, liver disease, or certain cancers. This pill does NOT protect you from sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Stop taking it and call your doctor right away if you have severe chest pain, sudden severe headache, vision changes, or leg pain or swelling.
typical_dosing: You take one pill by mouth every day at the same time each day. Most packs are 28 days — you take active hormone pills for 21 or 24 days, then take reminder (placebo) pills for the remaining days to keep your habit going. Try to take it at the same time every day to make it as effective as possible. If you miss a pill, follow the instructions in your package or ask your pharmacist what to do.
